title: The journey of one web request
purpose: Show the order of the network steps behind every page load, so each later page has a place in one picture.
explanation: The browser first checks its own cache. A fresh stored copy answers at once, with no network. On a miss, DNS gives the server IP address. The browser connects and encrypts: TCP plus a TLS handshake, or QUIC for HTTP/3, which includes TLS. It sends an HTTP request with headers and cookies. A CDN edge server near the user can answer from a fresh copy; otherwise the origin builds a compressed response. Every path ends at the response.
alt: Flowchart with seven nodes. A first decision asks whether the browser cache has a fresh copy; if yes, the response comes straight from it with no network. If no, DNS turns the name into an IP address; the browser connects and encrypts with TCP plus TLS, or QUIC with TLS built in; it sends an HTTP request with headers and cookies. A second decision asks whether the CDN edge server has a fresh copy. If yes, the CDN sends the response; if no, the origin server builds a compressed response. All paths end at the response, where the page renders.

learning_check.question: A second visit to a page sends no network request at all, and the page still shows. Which step answered, and what would make the browser go on to DNS and the CDN instead?
learning_check.answer: The browser cache answered with a fresh stored copy, so the trip stopped at the first decision. When that copy is missing or stale (its Cache-Control lifetime has passed), the browser goes on to DNS, connects, and sends the request, and then a fresh CDN copy or the origin answers.

title: How a cache answers one request
purpose: See the three outcomes of a cache lookup: fresh hit, validated reuse, or full fetch.
explanation: A cache first matches the URI and Vary fields. A fresh match is served at once. A stale match is checked with the origin: a 304 reuses the stored body, a 200 replaces it.
alt: Flowchart: a request is matched against stored responses by URI and Vary. No match goes to the origin. A fresh match is served with an Age header. A stale match sends a conditional request; a 304 updates the stored headers and reuses the body, a 200 brings a new response.

learning_check.question: What does a cache do with a stale response that has an ETag?
learning_check.answer: It sends If-None-Match; a 304 lets it reuse the stored body, a 200 replaces it.

title: The full TLS 1.3 handshake in three phases
purpose: Show which message belongs to which handshake phase and where encryption starts.
explanation: The client sends a ClientHello with a key share. The server answers with a ServerHello and its own key share, and both sides can now derive keys. From this point every handshake message is encrypted. The server sends EncryptedExtensions, then its Certificate, a CertificateVerify signature and a Finished MAC. The client answers with its Finished message, and application data can flow. Optional messages such as client certificates are left out.
alt: Sequence diagram between client and server: ClientHello with key share, ServerHello with key share, a note that everything after is encrypted, then EncryptedExtensions, Certificate with CertificateVerify and Finished from the server, Finished from the client, and finally application data.

learning_check.question: In the Network or Security view, the handshake takes one round trip before the first request. Which messages carry the key exchange, and which prove the server owns its certificate?
learning_check.answer: ClientHello and ServerHello carry the key shares. The server's CertificateVerify signature proves it holds the private key for its certificate, and Finished confirms the handshake was not altered.

title: Why HTTP/3 avoids transport head-of-line blocking
purpose: Show why one lost packet hurts every request on HTTP/2 over TCP but only one request on HTTP/3 over QUIC.
explanation: When one packet is lost, TCP holds back all data behind it, because it does not know which HTTP/2 streams are independent. In HTTP/3, each request uses its own QUIC stream and QUIC recovers loss per stream. Only the request that lost data waits.
alt: Flowchart: one lost packet leads to a transport choice. On HTTP/2 over TCP, TCP cannot see stream borders, so all active requests stall. On HTTP/3 over QUIC, loss is tracked per stream, so only the affected request waits.

learning_check.question: A page loads ten files over one connection and one packet is lost. Which files wait on HTTP/2 over TCP and which on HTTP/3?
learning_check.answer: On HTTP/2 over TCP, all ten can stall. On HTTP/3, only the file whose stream lost the packet waits.

title: From a URL string to a URL record, a serialization and an origin
purpose: Show that every URL string goes through one parser into a record of parts, and that the origin comes from that record, not from the raw text.
explanation: The basic URL parser reads the input string, with an optional base URL, and either fails or builds a URL record with eight fields. The serializer turns the record back into a string. The origin algorithm reads the same record: for http, https, ws, wss and ftp it returns a tuple of scheme, host and port, and for most other schemes it returns an opaque origin.
alt: Flowchart: an input string and optional base go into the basic URL parser. On failure, new URL throws. Otherwise the parser builds a URL record with scheme, username, password, host, port, path, query and fragment. The record feeds a serializer that produces href, and an origin step that gives a tuple origin for http, https, ws, wss and ftp, or an opaque origin for other schemes.

learning_check.question: Two URLs differ only in port: https://a.example/ and https://a.example:8443/. Are they the same origin, and which record field decides it?
learning_check.answer: No. The tuple origin contains scheme, host and port, and the port field differs (443 by default versus 8443).

title: jshttp/cookie: module map
purpose: Show how the four parts of the cookie library relate, so the learner knows where each rule lives.
explanation: The library has three code modules and one support slice. The header module reads and writes the Cookie header. The parse module reads Set-Cookie leniently. The serialize module writes Set-Cookie strictly. All three use shared rules and helpers in one file. The build slice guards them with a size limit, CI and benchmarks.
alt: Flowchart: three modules, cookie-header, set-cookie-parse and set-cookie-serialize, all point to a box of shared regular expressions and helper functions. A fourth box, build and infrastructure, points with dotted arrows at the three modules to show that it guards them.

learning_check.question: Which part decides how a bad Domain value is handled when you write a Set-Cookie header?
learning_check.answer: The set-cookie-serialize module checks the Domain against a regular expression and throws a TypeError.

title: jshttp/cookie: read a Cookie header, write a Set-Cookie header
purpose: Show the order of calls when a server reads the cookies of a request and sets one in the response.
explanation: Server code calls parseCookie with the Cookie header. Each value goes through defaultDecode, which returns the raw text if the percent escape is bad. The result keeps the first value of each name. Later, the server calls stringifySetCookie. It encodes the value, checks each attribute, and returns the header string. A bad attribute throws a TypeError.
alt: Sequence diagram: server code calls parseCookie, which calls defaultDecode for each value and returns an object. Server code then calls stringifySetCookie, which calls defaultEncode and returns the header string or throws a TypeError for a bad attribute.

learning_check.question: What happens when the Cookie header holds the value %1?
learning_check.answer: defaultDecode catches the error and returns the raw text, so parsing goes on and no exception reaches the server code.

title: nodejs/undici: module map
purpose: Show which part of undici does which job in the HTTP message path, so the learner knows where cache, version and cookie rules live.
explanation: Fetch handles headers, redirects and decoding. The cache interceptor sits between the caller and the network client and decides to reuse, revalidate or store. The dispatcher layer opens the connection and chooses HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 through ALPN. The cookie helpers work on Headers objects on their own. Tests guard the cache. Build and infra guard everything with CI and a release flow.
alt: Flowchart: fetch-and-compression points to cache-semantics and to http-versions-dispatcher; cache-semantics points to http-versions-dispatcher. Dotted arrows: cookies to fetch, cache-tests to cache-semantics, build-and-infra to the dispatcher.

learning_check.question: Which module decides whether the connection speaks HTTP/2?
learning_check.answer: http-versions-dispatcher: the connector offers ALPN protocols and Client picks connectH2 or connectH1 from the answer.

title: nodejs/undici: a cached GET that needs revalidation
purpose: Show the order of calls for one GET through the cache interceptor, the connector and the origin.
explanation: The cache interceptor builds a key and asks the store. A fresh entry is served at once with an Age header. A stale entry triggers a conditional request. The client connects, offers ALPN protocols, and the server picks h2 or http/1.1. A 304 keeps the stored body. A 200 replaces it.
alt: Sequence diagram: caller dispatches GET to the cache interceptor, which asks the store. On a fresh hit it answers directly. Otherwise it sends a conditional request through Agent and Client, the connector does TLS with ALPN, the origin answers 304 or 200, and the store is updated.

learning_check.question: What does the interceptor do when the origin answers 304?
learning_check.answer: It checks the 304 (ETag, URL, Vary) and then serves the stored body; a mismatch makes it refetch.

title: How TLS 1.3 sets up HTTPS in one round trip
purpose: See which messages a TLS 1.3 handshake sends, in what order, and why the browser can send its first request after one round trip.
explanation: Certificate says who the server claims to be, CertificateVerify proves that the server holds the private key, and Finished proves that nobody changed the handshake. Early data (0-RTT) saves one round trip but can be replayed, so send only requests that are safe to repeat.
alt: The browser sends ClientHello with a key share, the server name (SNI) and its application protocols (ALPN). The server replies with ServerHello and its key share, so both sides derive the same handshake keys. Everything after that is encrypted: EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify and Finished. The browser checks the signature and the MAC, sends its own Finished, and sends its first HTTP request. That is one round trip. A returning browser with a pre-shared key can send early data in the first flight, but that data has no forward secrecy guarantee and can be replayed between connections.

learning_check.question: Which handshake message proves that the server holds the private key for its certificate, and why is the Certificate message alone not enough?
learning_check.answer: CertificateVerify. It is a signature over the handshake transcript made with the private key. Anyone can copy a certificate, but only the key holder can make that signature.

title: How a browser cache reuses one response
purpose: See when a stored response is reused, revalidated with a 304, or fetched again from the origin.
explanation: A cache reuses a stored copy while its lifetime is greater than its age. After that it asks the origin, and a 304 answer keeps the copy.
alt: A browser asks for app.css. The first request misses and the cache stores the 200 response with max-age=60 and an ETag. At 30 seconds the copy is fresh and the cache answers alone. At 90 seconds the copy is stale, so the cache sends If-None-Match and the origin answers 304, which keeps the stored body.

learning_check.question: A copy has max-age=60 and is 90 seconds old. What does the cache send before it reuses the copy?
learning_check.answer: A conditional request with If-None-Match and the stored ETag. A 304 answer lets it reuse the stored body.

title: One lost packet in HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and HTTP/3
purpose: See at which layer head-of-line blocking happens in each HTTP version, and how ALPN picks the version.
explanation: Head-of-line blocking moves down a layer with each version: HTTP/2 removes it from HTTP, and HTTP/3 removes it from the transport by using QUIC streams instead of one TCP byte stream.
alt: A page needs three files: A style.css, B app.js and C logo.png. HTTP/1.1 sends one request at a time per connection, so B and C wait behind A. HTTP/2 interleaves all three as frames on one TCP connection, but when one TCP packet is lost, TCP holds back every byte after the gap, so all three stall. HTTP/3 gives each request its own QUIC stream, and QUIC recovers loss per stream, so only A waits. The version is chosen with ALPN during the TLS handshake: the client offers names, the server picks one. A server advertises h3 with Alt-Svc, and clients fall back to TCP when UDP is blocked.

learning_check.question: One packet that carries part of response A is lost. Which responses wait on HTTP/2 over TCP, and which on HTTP/3?
learning_check.answer: On HTTP/2 over TCP, A, B and C all wait, because TCP releases bytes only in order. On HTTP/3, only A waits, because each QUIC stream recovers its own loss.

explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Predict which responses stall after one lost packet in each HTTP version, and explain why.

On HTTP/1.1, B and C wait behind A on the connection. On HTTP/2, all three stall because TCP releases bytes only in order. On HTTP/3, only A waits because each QUIC stream recovers its own loss. The walkthrough ends with ALPN and Alt-Svc, which choose the version. A stepper lets the learner replay the loss in each version.

learning_check.question: On HTTP/2, one TCP packet that carries a frame of response A is lost. Which responses stall?
learning_check.answer: A, B and C. HTTP/2 streams share one TCP byte stream. TCP releases bytes only in order, so the bytes of B and C that arrived after the gap wait until the lost packet is retransmitted.

title: Choosing a realtime transport by who sends
purpose: Show how the direction of the data and the tolerated delay pick polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events or WebSocket.
explanation: If only the server sends text updates, Server-Sent Events keep one HTTP response open and push each event at once. If both sides send at any time, WebSocket is the transport that carries messages both ways on one connection. If some delay is fine, periodic polling batches updates into fewer requests. Long polling is the fallback when EventSource is not available.
alt: Decision flowchart. Question: who needs to send live data? Only the server with text leads to Server-Sent Events. Both sides at any time leads to WebSocket. Server with tolerated delay leads to periodic polling. From Server-Sent Events, a branch for no EventSource support leads to long polling.

learning_check.question: A chat app must send the user's messages and receive other people's messages. Which transport does the diagram pick, and why?
learning_check.answer: WebSocket, because both sides send at any time and WebSocket carries messages in both directions on one connection.

title: Change the cache headers and watch the outcome
purpose: Predict how max-age, no-cache, no-store, heuristics, s-maxage, Vary and hashed file names change hit, revalidate and miss.
explanation: Every scene loads a matching preset in the simulation, so you can step through the same rule request by request.
alt: The walkthrough steps through seven cache rules. max-age sets a lifetime; a stale copy revalidates with If-None-Match. no-cache stores but always revalidates, while no-store never stores. Without max-age a cache may guess about 10% of the time since Last-Modified. s-maxage gives shared caches such as a CDN their own lifetime. Vary keeps one copy per request header value. Hashed file names with a one-year max-age and immutable get a new cache key on every build.

learning_check.question: Why does a new hashed file name always cause a miss, even when the old file is cached for a year?
learning_check.answer: The cache key includes the URL. A new name is a new URL, so the cache has no stored copy for it.

title: Three questions decide every cached response
purpose: Connect the cache key, the freshness check and revalidation into one decision for HTML pages and hashed assets.
explanation: The key, the lifetime and the validator together decide hit, revalidate or miss for every request.
alt: A cache answers three questions in order: is there a stored copy for this key, is it fresh, and if not, does the origin answer 304 or 200. The directives set the answers: no-store, no-cache, max-age and s-maxage. A common pattern gives HTML no-cache with an ETag and hashed assets a one-year max-age with immutable.

learning_check.question: Which header set fits an HTML page that must never show an old version but should stay cheap to check?
learning_check.answer: Cache-Control: no-cache with an ETag, so every reuse is a small conditional request that usually ends in 304.

title: A request crosses the internet as packets
purpose: Show that a request travels as packets through routers, that TCP spends one round trip on a handshake, and that TCP resends a lost packet before the browser can read later bytes.
explanation: Before any HTTP data moves, TCP runs a three-way handshake: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. That costs one full round trip. The request and the response then cross the routers of several networks as separate packets. When a packet is lost, the server sends it again, and TCP holds back later bytes until the gap is filled. Reliable order costs time on a lossy network.
alt: Sequence diagram with three participants: browser, ISP routers and web server. The browser sends SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, the browser sends ACK, so one round trip passes before data. The browser sends the GET request; the server sends response packet 1, packet 2 is lost and sent again, and TCP delivers the bytes in order.

learning_check.question: The server is 100 ms away (one round trip). How long before the first HTTP request byte can leave the browser on a new TCP connection, and what happens to packet 3 if packet 2 is lost?
learning_check.answer: About 100 ms, because the TCP handshake takes one round trip first. Packet 3 waits in the receiver's buffer until packet 2 is resent, because TCP delivers bytes only in order.

title: Pick a realtime transport for each feature
purpose: Decide between periodic polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSockets for four product features: a notification feed, a stock ticker, a chat and a collaborative cursor.
explanation: Persistent connections remove the time a message waits for the next poll, but they do not make packets travel faster. Pick the simplest transport that matches the direction of the data.
alt: Two questions pick a realtime transport: who sends the data, and how much delay is acceptable. Polling asks on a timer, long polling holds the request open, Server-Sent Events stream text from the server, and WebSockets carry messages both ways. Four deep dives apply the questions to a notification feed, a stock ticker, a chat and a collaborative cursor.

learning_check.question: A notification feed only pushes short text events from the server. Which transport fits best, and why not WebSockets?
learning_check.answer: Server-Sent Events: the data goes one way and is text, and the browser reconnects automatically. WebSockets also work, but the application must then build its own reconnects and state handling.

title: Choose a realtime transport for each feature
purpose: Pick polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events or WebSocket for a product feature and justify the choice by data direction and tolerated delay.
explanation: Choose a path through the deck and open the deep dives. Pick polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events or WebSocket for a product feature and justify the choice by data direction and tolerated delay.
alt: A branching deck compares periodic polling, long polling, Server-Sent Events and WebSocket by who sends the data and how much delay is acceptable, shows the bandwidth cost of short polling intervals, and opens four deep dives: a notification feed, a stock ticker, a chat and a collaborative cursor.

learning_check.question: 10,000 clients poll every 60 seconds and get no new messages. They switch to every 1 second. What happens to the traffic the server receives?
learning_check.answer: It rises about 60 times, to over 60 Mbps. Each empty check still costs about 850 bytes of HTTP overhead. Sixty times more requests give about sixty times more traffic, so short intervals are expensive.

title: Which checks a stored cookie passes before a request carries it
purpose: Show the Domain, Path, Secure and SameSite checks that decide whether a request carries a stored cookie.
explanation: A request carries a stored cookie only when every check passes. Domain decides the hosts: without it, only the host that set the cookie. Path must contain the URL path. A Secure cookie needs https. For a cross-site request, Strict never goes, Lax goes only on a top-level navigation with a safe method such as GET, and None always goes but needs Secure. HttpOnly does not change sending; it hides the cookie from document.cookie.
alt: Decision tree: a stored cookie goes through a Domain check, a Path check and a Secure check. A same-site request then sends it. A cross-site request checks SameSite: Strict is not sent, Lax is sent only on a top-level GET navigation, None is sent. A final note says HttpOnly hides the cookie from document.cookie but it is still sent.

learning_check.question: A cross-site image request goes to shop.example.com. Which SameSite value lets the cookie travel?
learning_check.answer: Only None, because an image is not a top-level navigation, so Lax and Strict cookies stay home. Some browsers also block third-party cookies by default.

title: How a resolver finds the IP address for developer.mozilla.org
purpose: Show the fixed order of a DNS lookup on a cache miss, and that the TTL of the answer decides how long the resolver reuses it.
explanation: On a cache miss, the recursive resolver asks three kinds of server in turn. The root server points to the .org TLD servers. The TLD server points to the nameservers of mozilla.org. The authoritative nameserver returns the A record with its TTL. The resolver gives the IP address to the browser and keeps the answer until the TTL ends. TTL 300 s is the Cloudflare default and is an example value here.
alt: Sequence diagram with five participants: browser, recursive resolver, root server, .org TLD server and mozilla.org nameserver. The resolver misses its cache, asks the root, which refers it to .org, which refers it to the mozilla.org nameserver. That server returns an A record with TTL 300 seconds. The resolver returns the IP to the browser and caches it until the TTL ends.

learning_check.question: A second user asks the same resolver for developer.mozilla.org 2 minutes later. Which servers does the resolver contact?
learning_check.answer: None. The cached A record still has about 180 seconds of TTL left, so the resolver answers from its cache.

title: How the browser picks the cookies for one request
purpose: Apply the Domain, Path, Secure and SameSite checks to decide which stored cookies one request carries.
explanation: A request carries a stored cookie only when the host matches Domain, the path matches Path, the scheme satisfies Secure, and SameSite allows the request context. HttpOnly changes what JavaScript can read, not what the request carries.
alt: A browser stores five cookies from shop.example.com. For each request it checks Domain (which hosts), Path (which URL paths), Secure (https only) and SameSite (Strict, Lax or None against same-site and cross-site requests). HttpOnly hides a cookie from page scripts but the cookie is still sent. The __Secure- and __Host- name prefixes force safe attributes.

learning_check.question: A form on another site sends a POST to shop.example.com. Which SameSite value lets the cookie go with it?
learning_check.answer: Only SameSite=None (with Secure). Strict never goes cross-site, and Lax goes cross-site only on a top-level navigation with a safe method such as GET, and POST is not safe.

learning_check.question: The copy has max-age=60 and ETag "v1" and is now 90 seconds old. The file has not changed. What happens?
learning_check.answer: The cache sends If-None-Match: "v1" and the origin answers 304. A stale copy needs validation before reuse. The cache sends the stored ETag in If-None-Match. The file is unchanged, so the origin answers 304 and the cache keeps the stored body.

title: Decide which cookies a request carries
purpose: Predict which stored cookies a request carries from Domain, Path, Secure and SameSite, and say what HttpOnly and the __Host- prefix change.
explanation: Step through an animated walkthrough, change the simulation and answer the checkpoints. Predict which stored cookies a request carries from Domain, Path, Secure and SameSite, and say what HttpOnly and the __Host- prefix change.
alt: A browser holds five cookies from shop.example.com with different Domain, Path, Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite attributes. A guided walkthrough explains each check, then a stepper runs the checks for seven cases: a same-site fetch, a cross-site link, a cross-site form POST, a cross-site image, a link to a same-site subdomain, a link to plain http, and a set of __Host- and __Secure- cookies that the browser stores or rejects.

learning_check.question: A form on news.other.org sends POST to shop.example.com/account/pay. Which of the five cookies does the request carry?
learning_check.answer: Only widget (SameSite=None). Lax allows a cross-site request only when it is a top-level navigation with a safe method. POST is not safe, so the Lax cookies stay home and Strict never goes cross-site. SameSite=None allows every request, so widget goes.

title: The parts of https://shop.example.com:8443/cart?id=7#top
purpose: Show which parts of a parsed URL form the origin, which parts do not, and how the host gives the registrable domain that a site uses.
explanation: The URL parser splits the string into named parts. Scheme, host and port together are the origin, so a change to any one of them gives a different origin. Path, query and fragment never change the origin. The registrable domain is the public suffix plus one label, here example.com. A site is the scheme plus the registrable domain, so it is wider than an origin.
alt: Flowchart of one URL split into six parts. A group labelled origin holds scheme https, host shop.example.com and port 8443. A second group, not in the origin, holds path /cart, query id=7 and fragment top. An arrow from the host leads to the registrable domain example.com, which the site uses, so subdomains share a site but not an origin.

learning_check.question: Do https://shop.example.com and https://shop.example.com:8443 have the same origin? Are they the same site?
learning_check.answer: Different origins, because the port is part of the origin (443 by default versus 8443). Same site, because the scheme and the registrable domain example.com match.

title: One HTTP request and its response, part by part
purpose: Show that a request and a response have the same parts: a start line, header fields, an empty line and an optional body. Only the start line differs.
explanation: The browser sends a request whose start line holds the method, the target and the version. Header fields follow, then an empty line. A GET has no body. The server answers with a status line, its own header fields, an empty line and the body. Accept asks for a format, and Content-Type names the format the server chose.
alt: Sequence diagram with two participants, browser and API server. The browser sends GET /api/cart HTTP/1.1 with Host and Accept headers and no body. The server answers HTTP/1.1 200 OK with Content-Type and Cache-Control headers and a JSON body, so both messages share one structure and differ only in the start line.

learning_check.question: Which part of the response tells the browser that the request worked, and which part tells it how to read the body?
learning_check.answer: The status code 200 in the start line says the request worked. The Content-Type header says the body is JSON.

title: DNS record inspector flow
purpose: Show how the inspector turns one domain name into five record lookups, a report and a list of findings.
explanation: main.ts calls inspectDomain, which runs queryType once for each of five record types through a Resolver interface. The real resolver uses node:dns; tests use a stub. The Report goes to analyze, which runs the TTL, CNAME and CAA checks, and formatReport prints the findings.
alt: Flowchart with four boxes: main.ts calls lookup.ts, which queries the Resolver for each record type, passes a Report to checks.ts analyze, which passes a list of findings to report.ts formatReport for printing.

learning_check.question: Why can the tests run without a network?
learning_check.answer: queryType talks only to the Resolver interface, so tests pass a stub resolver instead of node:dns.

title: One request through a CDN
purpose: Show which layer of a CDN answers a request, where the cache key decides hit or miss, and what a purge removes.
explanation: The browser sends its request to a nearby point of presence (PoP), a CDN data center close to the user. The PoP builds a cache key; by default it is the full URL with the query string, plus a few headers such as Origin. On a hit it answers at once. On a miss it asks the origin and stores the response as its Cache-Control allows. A purge by URL or tag removes PoP copies only, so the next request refills from the origin.
alt: Flowchart: the browser sends a request to a nearby PoP. The PoP checks whether its cache key is stored. A hit goes straight back to the browser. A miss goes to the origin server, which returns the response with Cache-Control to the PoP. A dashed arrow shows the purge API removing PoP copies by URL or by tag.

learning_check.question: You purge /app.js by URL. A user who loaded it one hour ago opens the page again via a link, and their cached copy is still fresh. Which layer answers, and why?
learning_check.answer: The user's browser cache answers, because its copy is still fresh and a normal navigation reuses it. A CDN purge removes copies at the PoPs only; it does not reach browser caches.

title: Cache header auditor: from HAR file to report
purpose: Show how one HAR response becomes findings, so the learner sees which function owns each rule.
explanation: main.ts reads the HAR file and readEntries flattens each response into an Entry. auditEntry asks classify whether the entry is a hashed asset or HTML, and runs the matching grader. Both graders read Cache-Control through parseCacheControl. gradeVaryAndEncoding runs for every entry. main.ts prints each finding that is not ok.
alt: Flowchart: site.har goes to readEntries, then auditEntry, then classify. Hashed assets go to gradeHashedAsset and HTML goes to gradeHtml. Both call parseCacheControl. auditEntry also calls gradeVaryAndEncoding. All three graders feed the report in main.ts.

learning_check.question: Why does the auditor run gradeVaryAndEncoding for every entry but gradeHtml only for HTML?
learning_check.answer: Compression and Vary rules apply to any cacheable text response, while the freshness rules depend on the kind of file: hashed files may live a year, HTML must revalidate.

title: One request in REST, GraphQL and Connect RPC, and which one HTTP caches
purpose: Show where each API style puts its contract in the HTTP request, and why only GET requests, keyed by URL, fit HTTP caching.
explanation: HTTP identifies each resource by a URL (RFC 9110). A REST-style endpoint, simplified here, gives each resource its own URL, which HTTP caches and CDNs use as the cache key. GraphQL sends every operation to one endpoint, usually /graphql, with POST; only GET queries can be cached. Connect RPC posts to a URL named after the service and method, with JSON or Protobuf. A Connect method marked side-effect free can be sent as GET, so caches can store it too.
alt: Flowchart from a browser app to three endpoints. GET /users/42 goes to a REST endpoint, whose URL is the cache key for an HTTP cache or CDN. POST /graphql goes to a GraphQL endpoint, which reaches the cache only for GET queries, drawn as a dotted line. POST /Service/Method goes to Connect RPC, which sends JSON or Protobuf to server code; a dotted line shows that side-effect-free Connect methods sent with GET can also reach the cache.

learning_check.question: Why can a CDN cache GET /users/42 but not a GraphQL query sent as POST /graphql, and how can a Connect RPC call become cacheable?
learning_check.answer: HTTP caches use the URL of a GET request as the key. Every GraphQL POST goes to the same URL with the query in the body, so the URL does not identify the data; sending the query with GET puts it in the URL. Connect can send a method marked side-effect free as a GET request, which caches can store the same way.

title: gzip compared with Brotli and Zstandard
purpose: Let the learner choose a content coding for a static bundle and for per-request HTML, and see the size against CPU trade-off.
explanation: gzip works with every HTTP client, and undici asks for it even over plain HTTP. Brotli and Zstandard give smaller text bodies at high levels but cost more CPU, and undici asks for them over HTTPS only (lib/web/fetch/index.js:1586-1591 @ 011d947). So compress static files once at build time with a high level, and use a fast level for HTML built per request.
alt: Side-by-side comparison. Left, gzip: every client decodes it, it is offered even over plain HTTP, and it gives larger text bodies. Right, Brotli or Zstandard: smaller text bodies at high levels, high CPU cost at those levels, offered over HTTPS only. The verdict: pre-compress static files at build time and use a fast level for dynamic HTML.

learning_check.question: Why compress a hashed app.js at build time but HTML at request time with a fast level?
learning_check.answer: The hashed file never changes, so a slow high-level compression runs once and every user gets the smallest body. HTML changes per request, so slow compression would add CPU time to every response.

title: Cookie attribute linter flow
purpose: Show how the linter turns raw Set-Cookie header strings into findings and an exit code.
explanation: main.ts reads a text or HAR file with readSetCookieHeaders and passes the header strings to lintHeaders. For each header, parseSetCookie builds a cookie or returns null. lintCookie runs checkAttributes and checkPrefixes on the cookie. formatReport prints the findings and exitCode returns 1 when any finding is an error.
alt: Flowchart with five boxes in a row: input.ts readSetCookieHeaders, lint.ts lintHeaders, parse.ts parseSetCookie, rules.ts checkAttributes and checkPrefixes, then report.ts formatReport and exitCode.

learning_check.question: Why does the linter report a header with Max-Age=soon even though the parser accepts it?
learning_check.answer: The parser is lenient and drops the bad value into ignored; lintHeaders turns every ignored piece into a warning, so nothing is hidden.

title: Site network report: layers
purpose: Show the four layers of the capstone and that every dependency points inward to the domain.
explanation: main.ts creates every object. The interface layer (Cli and two renderers) calls the application layer (RunReport). RunReport and the infrastructure adapters both depend on the domain, which holds the six Check classes, the CacheControl and SetCookie parsers, Report and the port interfaces. The domain imports nothing from the other layers.
alt: Flowchart with six boxes. main.ts points to the interface layer and the infrastructure layer. The interface layer points to the application layer, RunReport. The application layer and the infrastructure layer both point to the domain layer with the six checks, parsers, Report and ports.

learning_check.question: Which layer would you edit to add a seventh check, and why does the infrastructure layer not change?
learning_check.answer: The domain layer: add one Check class. Infrastructure only reads files and does not know which checks exist.

title: Site network report: one run
purpose: Show one run from Cli to Report, including the invalid-input path and the crashing-check path.
explanation: Cli calls RunReport.execute. RunReport asks FileSiteDataSource to read dns.json, tls.json and site.har once, and JsonPolicyRepository to read policy.json. A missing or invalid file raises InputError and the Cli exits 2. Otherwise each Check runs on the same context; a check that throws becomes an unknown finding. Cli renders the Report and exits 0 or 1 by FAIL_ON.
alt: Sequence diagram with Cli, RunReport, FileSiteDataSource, JsonPolicyRepository and Check. Cli calls RunReport.execute, which loads the data and policy. An alt block shows InputError and exit 2 for bad files, or each check returning findings to RunReport, then Report to Cli, which renders it and picks exit 0 or 1.

learning_check.question: What does the report show if one Check class throws an exception?
learning_check.answer: An unknown finding for that check. The other checks still run, and the crash is never counted as a pass.

title: Site network report: run recipe
purpose: Show what the process reads and writes when it runs locally or in the Docker container.
explanation: The process is node src/main.ts, started by npm start or by the Dockerfile on node:26-slim. It reads settings from environment variables and four files from one input folder. It writes the report to stdout, JSON log lines to stderr, and exits with code 0, 1 or 2. It uses no network, database or queue.
alt: Flowchart with an environment-variable box and an input-folder box both pointing to the node process. The process points to three outputs: the report on stdout, JSON log lines on stderr, and an exit code of 0, 1 or 2.

learning_check.question: Why can a CI job use the exit code alone to block a launch?
learning_check.answer: Exit 1 means findings reached the FAIL_ON level and exit 2 means bad input, so only exit 0 lets the job pass.
